current_episode.title: Thinking About a Career in Construction? Inside Slippery Rock University's New Construction Management Program with Amanda McIsaac

guest.bio_context: Amanda McIsaac has worked in the construction industry for over 20 years with CDM Smith. She began as an adjunct professor at Slippery Rock University last year and is completing her second year teaching the newly launched Construction Management program. She has led the creation of multiple courses from scratch and established an advisory board of 12 industry professionals to guide curriculum development.

context.real_quote: Construction is relationships and while we have all of the technology to make our lives easier, when it comes down to it, it is relationship-based.
key_stats: Over 20 years in construction industry with CDM Smith
First cohort of 14 students in the Construction Management program
12 professionals on the advisory board, with 8 from Western Pennsylvania
Students complete OSHA 40-hour certification during junior year
One new course created in first year, three new courses created in second year
entities: Iron Mountain facility in Boyer's, Pennsylvania

pending_qa.q: How does a construction management program balance multiple specializations and career paths?
pending_qa.r: The Slippery Rock program has zero specialization, allowing students to explore different areas including highway construction, building, and residential work. The advisory board was shaped partly by student input on their career visions. Students are exposed to various roles through job site tours and guest speakers including owners, project managers, specialty contractors, and executives like the senior vice president for construction at UPMC.

pending_qa.q: What is the most critical gap identified by construction industry professionals in new graduates entering the field?
pending_qa.r: According to feedback from the first board meeting in March, communication was identified almost unanimously as a major gap. Industry professionals noted that new graduates often rely on abbreviated text messages and ChatGPT-generated emails, but construction is relationship-based and requires effective communication with subs, material suppliers, and field teams.

pending_qa.q: How does integrating OSHA 40-hour certification into the junior year benefit construction management students?
pending_qa.r: Students earn their 40-hour OSHA certification during their junior year, allowing them to go directly onto job sites with boots on the ground on day one of internships. This also enables the class to visit active project sites and understand jobsite safety protocols as visitors and guests, which is important for preventing accidents due to distraction or awe when observing construction activities.

pending_qa.q: What unique advantages does a career in construction management offer compared to other engineering disciplines?
pending_qa.r: With construction, students have the opportunity with their hands to build something and see progress almost daily, from nothing to a finished product. Unlike some other engineering paths, construction offers constant variety—after finishing one project that may last one or two years, students move to a new job and new project, constantly making and bettering communities and environments.

pending_qa.q: How is Slippery Rock University integrating real campus projects into the construction management curriculum?
pending_qa.r: The program works closely with Juan Perez, head of facilities, on actual university projects. Freshmen put together a proposal for work at Storm Harbor equestrian facility, and junior-seniors did similar work on Morrow Fieldhouse. Students receive actual blueprints, attend site walks, ask questions, and see how amendments are submitted and bids are calculated—giving them experience with real projects being bid by the university.

pending_qa.q: What role does mentorship play in shaping construction management careers according to industry experience?
pending_qa.r: Amanda McIsaac credits her long-term mentor for her career development over 15 years, noting he pushed her out of her comfort zone while fully supporting her and allowing her to learn from mistakes. She believes mentorship is overlooked and plans to have her mentor call in to meet her sophomores, as it is valuable regardless of career field and especially important for newer graduates unless their company has a formal program.
